deficits.label: Where ADHD brains tend to underperform neurotypical brains
deficits.description: These are the most consistently replicated findings, mostly rooted in executive function research.

items.name: Sustained attention on low-stimulation tasks
items.description: Not attention in general — attention regulation. ADHD brains struggle specifically when a task is boring, repetitive, or has delayed rewards (paperwork, long lectures, admin work).

items.name: Working memory
items.description: Holding multiple pieces of information in mind while manipulating them — this shows up reliably across studies and is one of the more 'core' deficits, not just a symptom.

items.name: Response inhibition / impulse control
items.description: The classic 'stop-signal' and 'go/no-go' lab tasks show ADHD brains are slower and less consistent at suppressing an automatic response.

items.name: Time perception and time management
items.description: People with ADHD are measurably worse at estimating how much time has passed or how long a task will take — this isn't just disorganization, it's a distinct perceptual difference (sometimes called 'time blindness').

items.name: Emotional regulation
items.description: Less talked about publicly, but heavily studied — ADHD is associated with faster, more intense emotional reactions and slower return to baseline, which isn't in the official DSM criteria but shows up in nearly every clinical review.

items.name: Task-switching costs
items.description: Ironically, despite the 'can't focus' stereotype, switching away from an engaging task is often harder for ADHD brains than switching between boring ones — the cost of interruption is higher.

items.name: Consistency/variability
items.description: ADHD performance isn't uniformly worse, it's more variable — same person can do brilliantly on a task one day and poorly the next. Researchers call this 'intra-individual variability,' and it's one of the most robust findings in the field.

strengths.label: Where ADHD may outperform or differ favorably
strengths.description: This side of the research is real but much younger, smaller, and more mixed than the deficit literature — worth being honest about that asymmetry.

items.name: Divergent thinking / idea generation
items.description: The most consistently replicated 'strength' finding. Multiple studies using tasks like the Alternate Uses Task show people with higher ADHD trait levels generate more original, unusual ideas — likely linked to reduced 'latent inhibition' (less automatic filtering of irrelevant associations), which lets more distant concepts connect.

items.name: Hyperfocus
items.description: Well-documented as self-reported and increasingly studied empirically — the same dopamine-driven attention system that makes boring tasks hard can lock onto highly stimulating or personally meaningful tasks with unusual intensity and duration.

items.name: Response to novelty and reward-seeking
items.description: ADHD brains show heightened sensitivity to novel stimuli, which correlates with real-world entrepreneurial and risk-taking behavior — genuinely useful in fast-changing, high-variance environments, genuinely costly in stable, rule-bound ones.

items.name: Real-time improvisation under pressure
items.description: Less formally studied, but a few papers touch on faster context-switching under high-stakes, high-stimulation conditions (crisis response, live performance) — plausibly connected to the same system that causes distractibility in low-stimulation settings.

caveat.title: The honest caveat
caveat.content: The 'deficit' literature and the 'strengths' literature are not equally rigorous. The weaknesses are established through decades of controlled lab tasks (working memory tests, go/no-go tasks) with large sample sizes. The strengths research is newer, often self-report based (people with ADHD describing their own strengths in surveys) rather than performance-based, and creativity studies in particular have mixed and sometimes contradictory results depending on which creativity measure is used. If you're building this into a visualization, I'd frame the weaknesses as 'measured performance differences' and the strengths as 'an emerging and less settled area of research' — treating them with equal confidence would overstate the evidence on one side.
